title: Consumer Reports: same ride, different prices on Uber and Lyft
hook: 174 volunteers requested 'identical' rides and saw a median gap of 42%.
collected: Trip requests; the companies acknowledge using personal data for promotions.
inferred: Prices and which promotions to show.
done: Consumer Reports had 174 volunteers in March-April 2026 compare fares for matching trips. It reported a 42.4% median gap between lowest and highest quotes and found 12.4% of displayed discounts were illusory.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Investigation REPORTED by Consumer Reports; both companies dispute the method. Press coverage often cites different figures (such as 50% or 11%). These are CR's own.

companyResponse.text: Uber: the findings are "based on a flawed methodology" and it "does not personalize prices, period". Lyft: "We do not engage in surveillance pricing."
companyResponse.source: Uber newsroom; Lyft statement via CR

outcome.text: Consumer Reports wrote to the FTC asking for an investigation; no FTC action found.

sources.title: Consumer Reports investigation reveals Uber and Lyft AI-driven pricing tactics

limits: Two requests a few seconds or metres apart are not perfectly identical. Prices change with supply and demand.
whyItMatters: A fake 'discount' is a pricing lever you can actually check.

title: Chicago ride-hail fares and neighbourhood demographics
hook: 100 million trips showed fares linked to who lives in a neighbourhood.
collected: City of Chicago public trip data (about 100 million trips) joined with census demographics.
inferred: Associations between fares and neighbourhood characteristics.
done: Pandey and Caliskan (AAAI/ACM AIES 2021) found fares were associated with neighbourhood share of non-white residents, poverty, age and education (effect sizes from small to medium).
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed analysis. It measured NEIGHBOURHOODS, not individuals, and is correlational.

sources.title: Disparate Impact of Artificial Intelligence Bias in Ridehailing Economy's Price Discrimination Algorithms

limits: Cannot separate demand and surge effects from bias; not evidence of personal profiling.
whyItMatters: An algorithm can have unequal effects even without anyone's personal data. Correlation is not intent.

title: India's CCPA notices to Ola and Uber over iPhone vs Android fares
hook: A viral post showed ₹290.79 on Android and ₹342.47 on iPhone for the same trip.
howObtained: Any app knows what phone it runs on.
done: After viral comparisons, the Central Consumer Protection Authority issued notices to Ola and Uber about alleged differential pricing based on phone model. The minister called it a 'prima facie unfair trade practice'.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Regulator notice, not a finding. In March 2025 the minister told Parliament both firms denied it. We found no published CCPA finding as of November 2026.

companyResponse.text: Uber: "We do not set prices based on a rider's phone manufacturer." It said pickup point, ETA and drop-off differed. Ola said it follows a homogeneous pricing structure and does not differentiate by phone for identical rides.
companyResponse.source: Company statements via Storyboard18 and Business Today

sources.title: Uber denies differential pricing based on phone models
Govt orders detailed probe into Ola, Uber over differential pricing

limits: Two phones in one moment can still differ in exact location, account history and offers.
whyItMatters: A good real example for learning how to test a claim fairly.

title: Uber said low-battery riders accept surge pricing more
hook: Uber's economist said people with a dying phone are more willing to pay surge, and that Uber doesn't use it.
collected: Battery level, which the Uber app reads for its own power-saving mode.
done: Keith Chen, then Uber's head of economic research, said on NPR's Hidden Brain that riders with low batteries are more likely to accept surge prices. He said Uber does not use battery level to set prices.
label: STATEMENT
labelNote: What an Uber insider said. There is NO evidence battery level is used in pricing.

companyResponse.text: Uber said it does not use battery level to set prices.

sources.title: This Is Your Brain on Uber
Uber knows you'll pay more for surge pricing when your battery is low

limits: The claim that battery drives prices is a myth built on this interview.
whyItMatters: Knowing something about you is not the same as using it.

title: India's CCPA flags 'advance tip' prompts in ride-hail apps
hook: Tip before the ride to be matched faster, which the regulator called exploitative.
inferred: Who will pay extra for speed.
done: The CCPA issued a notice to Uber (and reportedly scrutinised Ola and Rapido) over prompts nudging riders to tip in advance for faster service.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Regulator notice; no final order found.

companyResponse.text: Uber said it continues to engage with authorities and had made app changes.

outcome.text: Minister Pralhad Joshi: 'Forcing or nudging users to pay a tip in advance for faster service is unethical and exploitative.' No final order found.

sources.title: CCPA flags Uber's advance tip feature as unfair trade practice

whyItMatters: India's dark-pattern rules applied to an everyday app.

title: 'Algorithmic wage discrimination': how app workers describe their pay
hook: Two drivers doing the same work can be offered different pay, and neither can see why.
collected: Drivers' acceptance history, hours, locations and behaviour.
inferred: The lowest pay each driver is likely to accept, as drivers and the author describe it.
done: Law professor Veena Dubal, drawing on about nine years of fieldwork with ride-hail drivers, argues platforms use granular data to set personalised, variable and opaque pay. She calls for a ban.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Legal scholarship based on ethnography (interviews and observation). It is qualitative, not a pay audit.

sources.title: On Algorithmic Wage Discrimination, 123 Colum. L. Rev. 1929

limits: Describes experiences and logic; does not measure pay differences statistically.
whyItMatters: Pricing machinery can point at workers as well as customers.

title: Drivers' own data shows Uber's take rising under dynamic pay
hook: 258 UK drivers used data-access rights to audit 1.5 million of their own trips.
collected: Trip and pay records, obtained by drivers under GDPR data-access rights.
howObtained: Subject access requests via Worker Info Exchange.
inferred: Changes in hourly pay and the platform's cut.
done: Researchers (FAccT 2025) reported drivers' hourly pay fell from £22.20 to £19.06 after dynamic pay was introduced, and Uber's cut rose from about 25% to as high as 50% on some trips.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed study, but the sample is self-selected, and Uber disputes the figures.

companyResponse.text: Uber: "We do not recognise the figures in this report."

sources.title: Algorithmic pay audit of Uber drivers (FAccT 2025)
Uber rejects University of Oxford study

limits: 258 volunteers may not represent all drivers.
whyItMatters: Data-access rights let outsiders audit a black box. India's DPDP Act is due to give similar rights from about May 2027.

title: Fairwork India ratings of gig platforms
hook: Ola, Uber and Porter scored 0 out of 10 on fair-work principles.
howObtained: Researchers assess evidence on pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation.
done: Fairwork India 2024 rated 11 platforms using desk research, platform evidence and interviews with 440 workers. BigBasket, Swiggy, Urban Company and Zomato scored highest at 6/10; Ola, Porter and Uber scored 0. No platform showed that all its workers earn a local living wage after costs.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Academic-led ratings project with a published method.

outcome.text: Ratings published. Rajasthan (2023) and Karnataka (2025) have since passed gig-worker welfare laws.

sources.title: Fairwork India’s sixth report examines the changing nature of platform work

limits: A score reflects evidence the platform provided or researchers found; low scores can mean no evidence offered.
whyItMatters: Algorithmic management is a labour issue as well as a technology issue.

title: Uber's 'Greyball' tool evaded regulators
hook: Uber used data about users to spot city officials and show them a fake version of the app.
collected: User data such as location, payment details and app behaviour.
inferred: Whether a user was likely to be a regulator or enforcement officer.
done: The New York Times reported Uber used 'Greyball' to identify suspected officials and show them phantom cars or deny them rides. A Portland audit found 17 blocked accounts, 16 of them officials.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Reported by the NYT; Uber acknowledged the tool and said it would stop using it against regulators (company admission).

companyResponse.text: Uber's chief security officer said the company was "expressly prohibiting" its use to target regulators.

outcome.text: A federal grand-jury subpoena was reported in 2017; no public outcome found.

sources.title: How Uber Deceives the Authorities Worldwide

limits: No public legal resolution of Greyball.
whyItMatters: Profiling can be pointed at anyone, including regulators.
